Ruled out: total_nodes() is defined as 'hosts + switches count', deliberately excluding controllers (base Mininet keeps controllers in a separate list). 10 — if DockerHosts were double-counted (once in hosts, once in a separate containers/dockers list) -> 5+3+2; a real implementation bug I want the test to catch, hence exact equality rather than a range. 4 — only regular hosts + switches, treating containers as non-nodes. 5 — host-only count (2+3), ignoring switches. 9 or 11 — if links or interfaces leaked into the node count. All rejected.

values.formula: DockerHost class constants (spec-fixed): STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0, HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0. DockerHost.startup_time_ms = STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0 ms (image pull + namespace/cgroup setup). Plain Host startup = HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0 ms. startup_overhead_ratio() = 500.0 / 10.0 = 50.0 exactly (both operands exact binaries). Printed with :.2f -> '50.00'. Interpretation: a container host boots 50x slower than a namespace-only host — the Containernet paper's headline startup-cost point. Test assertion I would have written: abs(parsed - 50.0) <= 0.5, deliberately tight enough to reject the 51.0 additive reading.
values.alternatives: 51.00 — ADDITIVE/INCLUSIVE convention: if startup_time_ms returns HOST_STARTUP_MS + STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 510.0 (a container is a host PLUS container setup), ratio = 510/10 = 51.0. This is the ONE genuinely free design choice in this module and the only key I would flag as not hard-pinned by the text. I pick 50.0 because (a) the constant is literally named STARTUP_*OVERHEAD*_MS, read most simply as the container's own startup figure, (b) it is the simplest formula, and (c) 50 is a round designed-looking benchmark number whereas 51 looks like an artifact. 49.00 — EXCESS-over-baseline convention: (500-10)/10 = 49.0, the ratio of the extra overhead to host startup; a plausible reading of 'overhead ratio' but less canonical. 490.00 / 500.00 — reporting an absolute delta in ms (500-10) or raw container startup instead of a dimensionless ratio; rejected, spec says 'ratio'. 0.02 — inverted ratio (10/500); rejected by the stated order 'DockerHost startup / Host startup'. 0.50 / 51.02 — seconds or percent unit conversions; unsupported.

result.conventions: 1) Per-switch throughput overhead: chosen COMPOUNDING (0.98**N) over LINEAR (1 - 0.02*N). Justification is cross-layer: containernet.yaml, written against the same netsim codebase, defines SFC throughput as "link_bw * product of all VNF throughput_factors", and netsim/utils.compute_path_loss_rate composes per-link degradation multiplicatively; mininet.yaml's own wording is "2% throughput reduction per switch hop", i.e. per-hop. Linear would give 900.00 instead of 903.92 — this is the single genuinely under-determined key. 2) Switch count on an iperf path = switches actually traversed (5 for LinearTopo(k=5) h1->h5), not inter-switch links (4); the key name IPERF_5SW and "through 5 switches" fix this. 3) Host selection: iperf uses Mininet's default first-and-last host; avg_rtt/pingAll use all distinct host pairs. 4) Dijkstra tie-breaking is irrelevant for every value here: LinearTopo and TreeTopo are trees, so each host pair has exactly one simple path, and netsim/graph.py's hop-count Dijkstra returns it deterministically. 5) TreeTopo depth semantics = Mininet's addTree recursion (hosts only at depth 0), so hosts = fanout**depth. 6) "Total nodes" = hosts + switches, excluding the controller, per the spec's parenthetical. 7) Ping loss is reachability-based (fraction of unreachable host pairs), not a composition of TCLink loss percentages; with no loss configured in configs.py both readings give 0.0 anyway. 8) Output formatting follows netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result: floats via '{:.2f}' (903.92, 0.00, 14.67), ints raw (20, 9); a test parsing with float() is insensitive to whether the two counts print as 20/9 or 20.00/9.00.

values.formula: LinearTopo(k=10) per spec = "h1-s1-s2-...-sN-hN (k switches, each with one host)" => switches = k = 10, hosts = k*n with n=1 default = 10. Total nodes (hosts + switches) = 10 + 10 = 20. (Links, not asked: 10 host links + 9 inter-switch links = 19.) Verified by construction with netsim/graph.py WeightedGraph: hosts 10, switches 10, total 20.
values.alternatives: 21 if the Mininet controller object (c0, added by build()) were counted as a node — the spec kills this by writing "Total nodes (hosts + switches)", and Topo holds no controllers at all. 30 if a reader mis-set n=2 hosts/switch (real Mininet signature is build(k=2, n=1)); n=1 is the spec's "each with one host". 19 if links were printed instead of nodes. As test author I assert == 20 exactly (integer, no tolerance).

values.formula: TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=3): hosts live at the leaves, so hosts = fanout**depth = 3**2 = 9. (Switches = (fanout**depth - 1)/(fanout - 1) = (9-1)/2 = 4: root s1 + 3 mid switches; total nodes would be 13.) Verified by a recursive addTree-style build: hosts=9, switches=4.
values.alternatives: 3 under the "depth counts node levels including the host level" convention (fanout**(depth-1) = 3**1). 13 if "hosts" were misread as total nodes. 27 under fanout**(depth+1). Canonical Mininet TreeTopo.addTree() recurses depth times and emits a host only at depth==0, giving fanout**depth = 9; sibling sdn_controller.yaml also builds rules over Tree(2,3) on that assumption. As test author I assert == 9 exactly (integer, no tolerance).

values.formula: LinearTopo(k=5), all links 1000 Mbps (configs.MININET_EXPERIMENTS['iperf_linear5']: k=5, link_bw=1000). Default iperf pair = (hosts[0], hosts[-1]) = (h1, h5). Hop-count shortest path (unique — the topology is a tree) = h1-s1-s2-s3-s4-s5-h5, i.e. 6 links and 5 switches traversed. Bottleneck bw = min(1000 x 6) = 1000 Mbps. Apply Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02 per switch hop, compounding: 1000 * (1 - 0.02)**5 = 1000 * 0.98**5 = 1000 * 0.9039207968 = 903.9207968 -> printed via print_result's '{:.2f}' as 903.92.
values.alternatives: THIS IS THE ONE KEY NOT PINNED BY THE TEXT ALONE. (a) compounding/multiplicative 1000*0.98**5 = 903.92 (chosen — matches containernet.yaml's explicit "link_bw * product of all VNF throughput_factors" and utils.compute_path_loss_rate's multiplicative composition; "2% reduction per switch hop" reads as per-hop compounding); (b) linear/additive 1000*(1 - 0.02*5) = 900.00; (c) counting only switch-to-switch hops (4 not 5): 922.37 multiplicative / 920.00 linear — ruled out by the key name IPERF_5SW and "through 5 switches"; (d) iperf over h1-h2 (2 switches): 960.40 / 960.00. Because 903.92 vs 900.00 cannot be separated from the prose, as test author I would write a bounded assertion — assert 895.0 <= v <= 910.0 (or approx(903.92, abs=5.0)) — admitting both dominant conventions while rejecting the 4-switch (922) and 2-switch (960) readings. If a point value with tight tolerance is required: 903.92 +/- 0.01.

values.formula: TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=2) => 4 hosts (2**2), 3 switches, 6 links, graph connected (a tree). pingAll() = ping(all hosts): loss% = 100 * unreachable_pairs / total_pairs. Ordered pairs = 4*3 = 12 (unordered = 6); shortest_path returns a valid path for every pair, so unreachable = 0 => loss = 100*0/12 = 0.0%. Verified: 12 pairs, 0 unreachable. No per-link loss is configured (TCLink loss defaults to 0; configs.py 'tree_2_3' sets none), so there is no stochastic component.
values.alternatives: Ordered vs unordered pair counting, and including or excluding self-pairs, all yield 0.0 — the value is convention-independent because the numerator is zero. 100.0 would appear only if host-switch links were omitted or ping ran before build()/start(). A non-zero value (e.g. 5.88) would appear only if per-link TCLink loss were folded into pingAll, which the spec excludes by defining ping loss via shortest-path reachability. Formatting split: 0.00 as float (print_result '{:.2f}') vs 0 as int — a float()-parsing test accepts both. As test author I assert abs(v - 0.0) < 1e-6 (equivalently == 0).

values.formula: LinearTopo(k=4), every link delay = 2.0 ms (configs.MININET_EXPERIMENTS['linear4_rtt']: k=4, link_delay=2.0). Topology: 4 hosts, 4 switches, 7 links (4 host + 3 inter-switch). Paths unique (tree) => no tie-breaking ambiguity. Edges per pair = 2 + |i-j|; RTT = 2 * sum(link delays): h1-h2 3 links -> 6.0 one-way -> 12.0; h1-h3 4 -> 8.0 -> 16.0; h1-h4 5 -> 10.0 -> 20.0; h2-h3 3 -> 12.0; h2-h4 4 -> 16.0; h3-h4 3 -> 12.0. Sum = 12+16+20+12+16+12 = 88.0 over 6 unordered pairs => 88/6 = 14.666666... -> 14.67.
values.alternatives: Ordered-pair averaging (all_pairs_shortest_paths gives 12 ordered pairs) = 176/12 = 14.666666... — identical by symmetry, so pair-counting convention does not matter. 7.33 if the 2x round-trip factor were dropped (spec says "2 * sum of link delays", so ruled out). 20.00 if only the diameter pair h1-h4 were measured. 3.67 if the 1.0 ms config row were used instead of linear4_rtt's 2.0 ms (spec says "2ms link delay"). 13.33 if host-access links were excluded and only inter-switch hops counted. As test author I assert approx(14.67, abs=0.01) (or rel=1e-3 against 14.666667).

result.conventions:
TOPOLOGY (fixed, not a choice): Mininet TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=3) => switches = (3^2-1)/(3-1) = 4 (root s1 + leaves s2,s3,s4), hosts = 3^2 = 9 (3 per leaf), links = 9 host links + 3 core links = 12, total nodes = 13. Cross-checked against mininet.yaml Experiment 2 (MININET_TREE_HOSTS on Tree(2,3)), which only yields a sane value under this convention. A depth-3-style reading (13 switches / 27 hosts) is excluded by that cross-layer anchor.

PAIR ORDERING (chosen: ordered pairs, 9*8 = 72): the already-shipped helper /workspace/netsim/graph.py WeightedGraph.all_pairs_shortest_paths emits one entry per ORDERED (src,dst) with src != dst, and compute_all_paths() in the spec is described as "paths between all host pairs", so the reference almost certainly iterates ordered pairs. Unordered pairs (36) would halve rule counts to 90 unless each pair installs both directions, which returns to 180 — so 180 is stable across that axis.

RULE GRANULARITY (chosen: one rule per SWITCH on the path, matching {src_ip,dst_ip}): install_path_rules(path, src_ip, dst_ip, priority) takes both IPs, so match keys are unique per pair and nothing dedups; FlowTable.install only rejects at capacity (4096, never reached — busiest switch holds 54). Hosts on the path get no rule because flow tables exist only for registered switches. A dst_ip-only match key (dedup) would collapse to 4*9 = 36; counting every path node would give 324.

DIJKSTRA TIE-BREAKING: irrelevant for exps 1, 2 and for the core-link-failure variant of exp 3, because a tree has exactly one path per pair. It only matters if an implementation adds redundancy (leaf-leaf link) before failing a link; graph.py breaks ties by heap order on (dist, node-name) i.e. lexicographic node name, and it keeps the FIRST discovered predecessor (strict `nd < dist[v]`), so lowest-numbered switch wins.

TIMING MODEL (chosen: linear, per-rule): rule_install_time_ms = 0.1 is explicitly "per rule installation", so total = rules * 0.1 (no compounding, no per-path or per-pair batching, no path-computation time added). Throughput is a pure rate, so it is invariant to how many of the 1000 packets are table hits vs misses.

FREE DESIGN CHOICES (not pinned by spec, configs.py, or any sibling requirement): (a) which link fails in exp 3, and whether handle_link_failure re-derives ALL paths or only the paths that traversed the dead link; (b) how many rules exp 5 installs, with what idle/hard timeouts, and at what simulated clock. I checked /workspace/netsim/targets/configs.py — there is no SDN_EXPERIMENTS block at all (only MININET_/WIFI_/CONTAINERNET_), so no config anchor exists for these two. As the test author I would have asserted exps 1, 2, 4 as exact/tight-tolerance equalities and exps 3 and 5 as RANGE/BOUND assertions (integer, > 0, <= the exp-1 total of 180), because a point value there would fail any equally-valid implementation.

OUTPUT FORMAT: netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result() renders floats as "%.2f" and ints bare, so integer-valued keys (1, 3, 5) print with no decimal point and float-valued keys (2, 4) print as 18.00 / 20000.00. A test parsing with float() handles both.

values.formula: Tree(depth=2,fanout=3): 4 switches (s1 root; s2,s3,s4 leaves), 9 hosts (3 per leaf). Ordered host pairs = 9*8 = 72. Same-leaf pairs = 3 leaves * (3*2) = 18, each path h->sLeaf->h contains 1 switch. Cross-leaf pairs = 72-18 = 54, each path h->sLeaf->s1->sLeaf'->h contains 3 switches. Total rules = 18*1 + 54*3 = 18 + 162 = 180. Per-switch cross-check: each leaf holds 6 (same-leaf) + 18 (src local, dst remote) + 18 (dst local, src remote) = 42; root holds all 54 cross-leaf pairs; 3*42 + 54 = 180. All under FlowTable capacity 4096 (max 54 on one switch), so install() never rejects. Predicted test assertion: exact integer equality == 180.
values.alternatives: 90 if the reference iterates UNORDERED host pairs (36) and installs one direction only. 360 if each ordered pair installs a forward AND a reverse rule per switch. 324 if a rule is (wrongly) installed for every node on the path including the two end hosts (18*3 + 54*5). 36 if match_fields is dst_ip-only so rules dedup per switch (4 switches * 9 distinct destinations). 1620 if TreeTopo(depth=2) were read as 3 switch levels (13 switches / 27 hosts) - excluded by the mininet.yaml Tree(2,3) host-count anchor.

values.formula: total_install_time() = total_rules_installed() * rule_install_time_ms = 180 * 0.1 ms = 18.0 ms exactly (180*0.1 is exact in IEEE754 double: repr == 18.0, no 17.999... artifact). Printed by print_result as a float => '18.00'. Predicted test assertion: abs(v - 18.0) <= 0.01 (or 0.05 / 1% relative).
values.alternatives: 9.00 under the unordered-pair convention (90 rules), 36.00 under bidirectional-per-pair (360 rules), 3.60 under dst_ip-only dedup (36 rules) - i.e. this key is entirely a linear echo of exp 1 and any exp-1 alternative propagates by *0.1. 7.20 if 0.1 ms is charged per PATH installed (72 paths) rather than per rule. Slightly higher values if path-computation time or a per-switch control-channel RTT were also added - the spec charges only per-rule, so no compounding/overhead term applies.

values.formula: FREE CHOICE - not pinned by the text. Canonical pick: fail one core link s1-s2 (a switch-switch link is what 'simulates failure' most naturally, and s1-s2 is the first core link built), then have handle_link_failure re-derive all host-pair paths and reinstall. Post-failure the tree splits into A={s2,h1,h2,h3} and B={s1,s3,s4,h4..h9}. Reachable ordered pairs = 3*2 (inside A) + 6*5 (inside B) = 6 + 30 = 36. Rules = A: 6*1 = 6; B: same-leaf 2 leaves*(3*2)=12 pairs *1 switch = 12, cross-leaf s3<->s4 = 3*3*2 = 18 pairs *3 switches = 54; so 6 + 12 + 54 = 72. Predicted test assertion (as the author, knowing this is unpinnable): a BOUND, e.g. isinstance(v,int) and 0 <= v <= 180, not an equality.
values.alternatives: 0 under 'recompute only the paths that traversed the failed link': 36 ordered pairs used s1-s2 and a pure tree has NO alternate route, so nothing can be reinstalled (verified by simulation). 108 if the metric counts rules INVALIDATED/needing reinstall rather than successfully reinstalled (36 affected pairs * 3 switches). 140 if the failed link is a host link h1-s2 instead of a core link, with full reinstall (8 reachable hosts: 14 same-leaf + 42*3 cross-leaf). 72 again (coincidence) if the experiment first adds a redundant leaf-leaf link s2-s3 and then fails s1-s2, rerouting only the 18 s2-host<->s4-host pairs over 4 switches each. 180 or 252 if the reported number is total_rules_installed() after recovery rather than the count installed during recovery (tables cleared vs not cleared).

values.formula: Spec pins 1000 packet-in events at 0.05 ms of controller processing each. Total simulated time = 1000 * 0.05 ms = 50 ms = 0.05 s. Throughput = packet_in_count / elapsed_s = 1000 / 0.05 = 20000 packet-ins per second. Equivalently 1 / (0.05e-3 s) = 20000 - the rate is independent of the packet count, so it is robust even if some of the 1000 packets are table hits rather than misses. Printed as float => '20000.00'. Predicted test assertion: abs(v - 20000.0) <= 1.0 (or 0.01 / 1% relative).
values.alternatives: 20.00 if 0.05 were misread as seconds per packet-in. ~1000-2000 if the reference also charges the 0.1 ms/rule installation time incurred by each reactive install into the elapsed time (e.g. 1 rule per packet-in => 1/(0.15 ms) = 6666.67; 3 rules per miss on the tree => 1/(0.35 ms) = 2857.14) - the spec's phrasing ('with 0.05 ms per packet-in') argues against mixing install time in. 20000 stands under every reading that treats 0.05 ms as the whole per-event cost.

values.formula: FREE CHOICE - the spec gives no rule count, no timeout value and no simulated clock for this experiment, and configs.py has no SDN_EXPERIMENTS block to supply them. Canonical/simplest self-contained demo consistent with FlowRule defaults (idle_timeout=0 / hard_timeout=0 meaning permanent): install 10 rules into one FlowTable, give every other rule idle_timeout=5 s (the other 5 stay permanent at 0), set last_matched_time = 0 for all, then call evict_expired(current_time=10.0, ...). 10/2 = 5 rules are past their idle timeout and are evicted; the 5 permanent rules survive. Predicted test assertion (as the author): a BOUND - isinstance(v,int) and 1 <= v <= rules_installed - because no point value is derivable from the text.
values.alternatives: 10 if all 10 installed rules carry a finite timeout that has elapsed (simplest 'everything expires' variant). 20 or 10 for a 20-rule batch (all-expire vs half-expire). 100 or 50 for a 100-rule batch. 180 or 90 if the experiment reuses the exp-1 proactive install on Tree(2,3) and expires all / half of those 180 rules. 0 if the simulated clock is not advanced past the timeout, or if hard_timeout semantics are measured from install time and the reference forgets to record install_time. 4 if only every 3rd of 10 rules is given a timeout. Any of these is defensible - the number of rules an experiment installs and the timeout schedule are pure implementation freedom here.

result.conventions:
FIXED BY SPEC/CONFIG (no freedom): (a) c = 3e8 exactly, as the spec literally writes `20*log10(4*pi*d*f/c) where c = 3e8`. Using the exact 299792458 shifts PL0 by only +0.006 dB and both printed values are unchanged at 2 dp, so this choice is harmless. (b) All propagation experiments use the LOG-DISTANCE model, not bare Friis: both `pathloss` and `signal_strength` entries in /workspace/netsim/targets/configs.py carry `path_loss_exp: 3.0` and `ref_distance_m: 1.0`, which only the log-distance model consumes. PL(d0=1m) = 20*log10(4*pi*1*2.4e9/3e8) = 20*log10(100.53096491) = 40.0459970 dB. (c) Antenna gains default to 0 dB — the spec writes `RSSI = tx_power + gains - path_loss` with gains as optional trailing args (`...`) and configs.py supplies no gain, so gains=0. Real Mininet-WiFi defaults antennaGain to 5 dBi per side, which would add +10 dB; I rejected that because configs.py never mentions gain. (d) Association uses min_rssi_dbm from the *matching* config block: -80.0 dBm for the `association` experiment, -75.0 dBm for the `mobility` experiment. Mixing these up is the single most likely implementation bug. (e) `netsim/experiments/__init__.py:print_result` formats floats with `:.2f` and ints bare, so PATHLOSS/SIGNAL/COVERAGE print with two decimals and ASSOC/HANDOVER print as bare integers.

DERIVED RANGE CONSTANTS: max_range solves tx - (PL0 + 10*n*log10(d)) = min_rssi, i.e. d = 10**((tx - min_rssi - PL0)/(10*n)). At min_rssi=-80: d = 10**((20+80-40.045997)/30) = 10**1.998467 = 99.6476 m. At min_rssi=-75: d = 10**((20+75-40.045997)/30) = 10**1.831800 = 67.8891 m. Both APs share tx_power/n/freq, so "strongest signal AP" reduces exactly to "nearest AP" — the association rule is purely geometric.

FREE DESIGN CHOICES I HAD TO PICK (experiments 4 and 5 only):
1. RandomWaypoint start position. configs.py `mobility` gives area, ap_positions, num_steps, speed_range, pause_time, seed — but NO start_pos. `generate_trace(start_pos, num_steps)` takes it as a caller argument. I chose the area centre (100.0, 100.0) = (area_width/2, area_height/2), the most common reference choice. This is the largest single source of variance in WIFI_COVERAGE_PCT.
2. Order of RNG draws per waypoint. I draw target x, then target y, then speed — matching the spec's own word order "move toward random target at random speed". Because area_width == area_height == 200.0, `rng.uniform(0,200)` twice, `rng.uniform(0,200,2)`, and `200*rng.rand()` all consume the legacy RandomState double stream identically, so only the target-vs-speed permutation matters, not the coding idiom. Drawing speed first shifts coverage by roughly +1 to +5 points.
3. Step semantics: one trace sample per unit time step, displacement = speed (dt = 1.0 s); on arrival (remaining distance <= speed) snap to the target and draw a fresh target+speed; pause_time=0 so no idle steps. `generate_trace` returns exactly num_steps=500 samples and does NOT prepend the start position. Tested alternatives (prepend start as a 501st sample; consume leftover distance within the same step toward the new target) leave the handover count at 4 and move coverage by at most 0.2 points.
4. Handover definition. I count only associated_ap transitions where BOTH the previous and current AP are non-None and different — i.e. real 802.11 roaming between two APs. Dropping out of coverage and later re-associating with the SAME AP is a re-association, not a handover, and is not counted. This is the question the task flagged, and it is the dominant lever on this value: the strict reading gives 4, counting every None->AP re-entry as well gives 10, and counting every change in the association variable including AP->None drops gives 17.
5. Tie-breaking / stickiness are non-issues here: I verified nearest-AP first-index-wins vs last-index-wins, and greedy-re-evaluation vs sticky-with-threshold-hysteresis, all yield handover=4 and coverage=82.00 on this trace. The only exact tie is the centre start point (equidistant 50 m from both APs), and it is never sampled because the first recorded sample is already one step of motion later.

ROBUSTNESS EVIDENCE: I swept 48 combinations of {2 draw orders} x {8 start positions} x {3 step semantics}. Strict handover count was 4 in 43 of 48 (3 in the other 5), so 4 is strongly modal. Coverage ranged 80.4%–88.2% with 82.00 modal for the centre-start/target-first family; the long-run stationary value for this geometry is ~77.9% (100k-step trace) and the 200-seed mean at 500 steps is 79.2%, confirming 82.00 is a plausible seed-42 sample rather than an artefact. The 500-step denominator forces every coverage value to be a multiple of 0.2.

CROSS-LAYER NOTE (not asked for, but it constrains the shared helpers): the Mininet core layer these WiFi values sit on top of has FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02 declared as a per-switch-hop factor, which for iperf through LinearTopo(k=5) implies the multiplicative reading 1000*0.98**5 = 903.92 rather than the linear 1000*(1-0.02*5) = 900.00. No WiFi value depends on it — WirelessLink derives bandwidth from an RSSI threshold table, not from switch overhead — but the same multiplicative-vs-linear question recurs in the Containernet SFC throughput experiment, where the spec settles it explicitly as "product of all VNF throughput_factors".

values.alternatives: Bare Friis at 50 m (ignoring path_loss_exp=3.0 from configs.py) = 20*log10(4*pi*50*2.4e9/3e8) = 74.0254 -> 74.03; identically, log-distance with n=2 collapses to Friis and also gives 74.03. Using the exact c=299792458 instead of the spec's c=3e8 gives PL0=40.052008 and PL(50)=91.021108, which still prints 91.02 — so that convention is invisible at 2 dp. Real Mininet-WiFi's own logDistance kernel (10*n*log10(d) + 20*log10(f_MHz) - 27.55) gives 40.0396 + 50.9691 = 91.01 (off by 0.01 from the spec formula because -27.55 is a rounded constant); I use the spec formula verbatim. If d0 were taken as 10 m rather than the configured 1.0 m, PL = 60.0460 + 30*log10(5) = 81.01.

With Mininet-WiFi's real default antennaGain=5 dBi on each side (+10 dB total) the value becomes 20 + 10 - 100.046 = -70.05; I rejected this because configs.py specifies no gain and the spec lists gains as an optional trailing argument. Bare Friis at 100 m (n=2) gives 20 - 80.0460 = -60.05. Exact c=299792458 gives -80.052008, which still prints -80.05. Note the near-coincidence that is worth not tripping over: this RSSI of -80.046 dBm sits marginally BELOW the association experiment's -80.0 dBm threshold, so a station at exactly 100 m would fail to associate — but that distance is not in the association distance list, so it never bites.

values.formula: 10 stations at distances [10,30,50,70,90,110,130,150,170,190] m from one AP; tx=20.0 dBm, n=3.0, f=2.4 GHz, min_rssi=-80.0 dBm (from the `association` block of configs.py). Coverage radius: max_range = 10**((tx - min_rssi - PL0)/(10*n)) = 10**((20.0 + 80.0 - 40.0459970)/30) = 10**1.99846677 = 99.6476 m. Per-station RSSI = 20 - (40.045997 + 30*log10(d)): d=10 -> -50.046 (pass); d=30 -> -64.360 (pass); d=50 -> -71.015 (pass); d=70 -> -75.399 (pass); d=90 -> -78.673 (pass); d=110 -> -81.288 (fail); d=130 -> -83.462 (fail); d=150 -> -85.324 (fail); d=170 -> -86.955 (fail); d=190 -> -88.410 (fail). Count of RSSI >= -80.0 is 5. Integer, so print_result emits bare -> 5
values.alternatives: The decisive free-ish choice is WHICH min_rssi is used. Correct per configs.py is the `association` block's -80.0 dBm -> 5. If an implementer wrongly reuses the `mobility` block's -75.0 dBm, the radius drops to 67.889 m and only d=10,30,50 pass -> 3. A -90 dBm sensitivity would admit all ten (radius 214.68 m) -> 10. Strict `>` instead of `>=` at the threshold changes nothing here since no station lands exactly on -80.000. If the geometry were reinterpreted as stations spread along a line with the AP centred rather than measuring radial distance, the count would change, but 'stations at distances 10-190m' plainly means radial distance from the AP. Adding the real 5+5 dBi antenna gains would push the radius to 214.68 m and give 10 — another reason the gains=0 convention matters.

values.formula: 500-step RandomWaypoint, numpy RandomState(seed=42), area 200x200, speed U(1,5) m/s, pause 0, start (100,100); 2 APs at (50,100) and (150,100), min_rssi=-75 dBm -> coverage radius 10**((20+75-40.045997)/30) = 10**1.8318 = 67.8891 m. At each of the 500 samples the station associates with the nearest AP within 67.8891 m (equal tx power makes strongest-RSSI == nearest), else None. The resulting association run-length sequence is 18 segments, as (ap, first_step): (AP1,0) (None,15) (AP1,43) (AP2,80) (None,119) (AP2,131) (AP1,135) (None,174) (AP1,182) (AP2,208) (None,212) (AP2,242) (None,270) (AP1,272) (None,395) (AP1,401) (AP2,423) (None,496). Counting only AP->AP transitions with no None in between: AP1->AP2 at step 80 (#1), AP2->AP1 at step 135 (#2), AP1->AP2 at step 208 (#3), AP1->AP2 at step 423 (#4). Total = 4. Integer -> prints 4
values.alternatives: The definition of 'handover' dominates this value, exactly as the task suspected. (a) Strict 802.11 roaming, prev and cur both non-None and different -> 4. This is what I chose: losing coverage and re-associating with the same AP is a re-association, not a handover. (b) Count every new association, i.e. any None->AP re-entry plus AP->AP -> 10. (c) Count every change of the associated_ap variable including AP->None disassociations -> 17. Secondary levers are far weaker: over a 48-way sweep of {target-first vs speed-first RNG order} x {8 start positions} x {3 step semantics} the strict count was 4 in 43 cases and 3 in 5 (speed-first order combined with a centre or top-edge start). Nearest-AP tie-breaking (first index vs last index wins) and greedy-vs-sticky association both leave it at 4, since the centre-point exact tie is never sampled. A random start drawn from the same RNG gives 5. Because start_pos is a caller argument that configs.py does not pin, this value is not fully determined by the spec; 4 is the modal and most canonical outcome.

values.formula: Same seed-42 trace as WIFI_HANDOVER_COUNT (500 samples, radius 67.8891 m, APs at (50,100) and (150,100)). Coverage = fraction of samples with a non-None associated AP. Summing the associated run lengths from the segment list gives 410 associated samples and 90 uncovered samples (the six None runs: steps 15-42 = 28, 119-130 = 12, 174-181 = 8, 212-241 = 30, 270-271 = 2, 395-400 = 6, 496-499 = 4; 28+12+8+30+2+6+4 = 90; 500-90 = 410). WIFI_COVERAGE_PCT = 100 * 410/500 = 82.0. Printed as '{:.2f}' -> 82.00
values.alternatives: This is the least spec-determined of the five, because it is a single short-sample statistic and configs.py never pins start_pos. Over the 48-variant sweep the value ranged 80.40 to 88.20, all multiples of 0.2 (the 500-step denominator); 82.00 is modal for the centre-start/target-first family and 87.60 is modal for the speed-first family. Concretely: start (100,100) target-first -> 82.00 (chosen); start (100,100) speed-first -> 83.20; start (0,0) target-first -> 80.80; start (0,0) speed-first -> 87.60; random start from the same RNG -> 82.40. Prepending the start position as a 501st sample gives 410/501 = 81.84 and dropping a step to keep 500 gives 82.20. A purely geometric reading — area of the two clipped radius-67.889 circles over the 200x200 box — gives only 61.10%, and the true long-run RandomWaypoint stationary value is ~77.93% (100k-step trace), both well below 82.00 because RandomWaypoint concentrates dwell time in the centre band where the two AP disks overlap; the 200-seed mean at 500 steps is 79.21%. So 82.00 is a legitimate seed-42 sample, not an artefact, but any grader must accept it as convention-dependent. If coverage were defined as time associated with a SPECIFIC AP rather than with any AP, or if the uncovered start segment were excluded from the denominator, the number would differ again.

values.formula:
Log-distance model, params from WIFI_EXPERIMENTS['pathloss'] in /workspace/netsim/targets/configs.py: freq_ghz=2.4 -> f=2.4e9 Hz, path_loss_exp n=3.0, ref_distance_m d0=1.0, test_distance_m d=50.0.

Step 1 - Friis loss at the reference distance (spec: 20*log10(4*pi*d*f/c), c=3e8):
  4*pi*d0*f/c = 4 * 3.14159265358979 * 1.0 * 2.4e9 / 3e8 = 100.53096491487338
  PL(d0) = 20*log10(100.53096491487338) = 20 * 2.00229985101404 = 40.0459970202808 dB

Step 2 - log-distance extension: PL(d) = PL(d0) + 10*n*log10(d/d0)
  10*n*log10(d/d0) = 10*3.0*log10(50.0/1.0) = 30 * 1.6989700043360187 = 50.96910013008056 dB

Step 3 - total:
  PL(50) = 40.0459970202808 + 50.96910013008056 = 91.01509715036136 dB

Printed via netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result(), which formats floats as '{:.2f}':
  -> 'WIFI_PATHLOSS_50M: 91.02'

Test assertion I would have written: exact match on the string '91.02', or float(v) == pytest.approx(91.015, abs=0.01).
values.alternatives:
Fully pinned by the spec text plus configs.py; every free knob is written down. Competing conventions and what each yields:

(a) HANDOVER = adjacent AP->AP transition, `prev` reset to None on a coverage gap (re-association to a different AP after a gap does NOT count): 4 in 144/224 variants, 3 in 52, 5 in 28. This is the most canonical: the spec gives Station an `associated_ap` attribute and MininetWifi.auto_associate() must clear it for count_associated() to be correct, so `prev` naturally becomes None during gaps. -> 4 (my pick).
(b) HANDOVER = sticky previous AP, so re-association to a DIFFERENT AP after a coverage gap counts: 5 in 104/224, 6 in 56. Under the canonical trace this yields 5 (the gap-ignoring AP sequence is AP0,AP0,AP1,AP1,AP0,AP0,AP1,AP1,AP0,AP0,AP1 = 5 changes). This is the second-most-likely intended answer and I regard 4 vs 5 as nearly a coin flip.
(c) HANDOVER = any re-association after a gap, including back to the SAME AP: 10.
(d) HANDOVER = any change of association state including to/from None (deassociation counted as an event): 17, or 18 if the initial association is also counted.
(e) Number of coverage gaps alone: 7.

result.conventions:
OUTPUT FORMATTING (fully determined, not a choice I made): /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py already ships print_result(name, value), which emits f'{name}: {value:.2f}' for floats and f'{name}: {value}' otherwise. So the three float keys print with exactly two decimals and the two count keys print as bare integers. Any test I wrote would parse 'KEY: VALUE' lines from stdout on that basis. This also means sub-0.005 differences (e.g. c=3e8 vs c=299792458) are invisible in the output.

PROPAGATION CONSTANTS (pinned by spec): c = 3e8 exactly, as stated in the requirement, not 299792458. Reference-distance path loss is Friis at d0, and d0 = ref_distance_m = 1.0 from configs.py, giving the constant PL0 = 20*log10(4*pi*2.4e9/3e8) = 40.0459970202808 dB that recurs in all five derivations. Antenna gains default to 0.0: the spec signature received_signal_strength(tx_power_dbm, freq_hz, distance_m, ...) hides them behind defaults and configs.py defines no gain keys anywhere. This matters most for WIFI_ASSOC_COUNT, where a total gain of +2 dB would flip the 110 m station into range and change 5 to 6.

PER-EXPERIMENT PARAMETER SCOPING (the main trap): configs.py gives each experiment its own dict, and the min_rssi threshold DIFFERS between them - association uses -80.0 dBm, mobility uses -75.0 dBm. The requirement prose only mentions '-75dBm', and only in the experiment-4 bullet. Applying -75 to the association experiment would yield 3 instead of 5. I scoped each experiment strictly to its own config dict.

LINEAR vs COMPOUNDING OVERHEAD: not applicable to this module. That convention question belongs to the Mininet core layer (Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02, where 0.98^N vs 1-0.02*N genuinely bites for MININET_IPERF_5SW). Nothing in the WiFi layer accumulates a per-hop penalty; path loss is additive in dB by definition and the 802.11g rate table is a plain lookup. Likewise Dijkstra tie-breaking is irrelevant here - no WiFi experiment routes a packet.

DETERMINISTIC vs TRACE-DEPENDENT SPLIT (the key finding): experiments 1-3 are closed-form and derivable from the requirement plus configs.py alone. I would have written exact equality assertions for them: 91.02, -80.05, 5, with a tolerance of about +/-0.01 on the floats (only needed to absorb c-constant and float-repr wobble) and no tolerance at all on the integer count. Experiments 4 and 5 are NOT derivable. The spec fixes seed=42, num_steps=500, the AP geometry and the -75 dBm threshold, but RandomWaypointMobility has at least five undetermined knobs - the station's starting position, the RNG draw order (target-then-speed vs speed-then-target), whether generate_trace() includes start_pos in the returned list, the arrival predicate (remaining <= speed vs < speed), and whether positions are clipped to the area - and 'handover' itself is left undefined.

HANDOVER DEFINITION (explicit choice): I count a handover only as a direct AP-to-AP change, treating a coverage gap as resetting the previous association to None, because the spec models association as Station.associated_ap state that auto_associate() must clear for count_associated() to work. That gives 4. The competing sticky convention, where re-association to a different AP after a gap still counts, gives 5. I consider 4 vs 5 close to a coin flip and would not assert either as an equality.

WHAT I WOULD HAVE ASSERTED AS A RANGE: WIFI_HANDOVER_COUNT and WIFI_COVERAGE_PCT. To quantify the exposure rather than guess, I swept 224 combinations of the undetermined mobility knobs at seed 42. Handover count stayed tightly bounded at 3-6 (mode 4 under my chosen definition, 5 under the sticky one), so a bound like 1 <= n <= 20 is safe. Coverage ranged 67.80-89.40 percent (median 82.30, canonical 82.00), so a bound like 50 <= pct <= 95 is safe while any tolerance tighter than roughly +/-5 percentage points would be untestable against an independent implementation. Two independent anchors confirm the canonical 82.00 is physically sensible: uniform-area geometric coverage of the two 67.89 m disks over the 200x200 square is 61.13 percent, and because RandomWaypoint is centre-biased and both APs sit on the centre line y=100, the long-run achieved coverage rises to 78.54 percent over 400k steps - with 82 percent being ordinary sampling noise at n=500.

1) Propagation constants taken verbatim from the spec: c = 3e8 (not 299792458) and Friis = 20*log10(4*pi*d*f/c); freq_ghz=2.4 is converted to 2.4e9 Hz. Both experiments 1 and 2 use the log-distance model with n=3.0 and d0=1.0 rather than plain Friis, because /workspace/netsim/targets/configs.py carries path_loss_exp=3.0 and ref_distance_m=1.0 in BOTH the 'pathloss' and 'signal_strength' blocks - keys only consumed by log_distance_path_loss. The choice of c moves results by ~0.006 dB, below printed precision.
2) Antenna gains: the spec writes 'RSSI = tx_power + gains - path_loss' but never names a gain constant, so the literalist reading is gains = 0 dB.
3) Association predicate: RSSI >= min_rssi_dbm (inclusive), strongest-RSSI AP wins, first AP in list order wins an exact tie. No station or trace sample lands exactly on a threshold, so inclusive-vs-strict and the tie-break are immaterial to all five values.
4) min_rssi is taken per experiment block, not globally: -80.0 dBm for WIFI_ASSOC_COUNT (the 'association' config) and -75.0 dBm for the mobility experiments (the 'mobility' config, matching the spec prose 'min_rssi=-75dBm'). Mixing them up is the largest single error source (it would turn 5 into 3).
5) Random waypoint is genuinely under-specified - the spec fixes only 'numpy RandomState with configurable seed', 'move toward random target at random speed, pick new target on arrival', seed=42, 500 steps, speed 1-5 m/step, 200x200 area, pause_time=0. I fixed the simplest canonical form: draw target (x then y, uniform over the area) then speed; one step = one time unit so displacement per step equals the speed in metres; on arrival (remaining distance < speed) snap onto the waypoint and draw the next target then speed; the trace is the 500 post-move positions; the station starts at the area centre (100,100) since no start_pos is given. Verified that vectorised target draws (rng.rand(2), rng.uniform(0,[W,H]), rng.uniform(0,W,2)) consume identical doubles from RandomState and give an identical trace.
6) Handover definition: a step where the previous and current associated APs are both non-None and differ. The competing 'last-known AP' convention (a re-association to a different AP after a coverage gap counts) yields 5; I chose immediate-previous because it is what the straightforward `prev = current` loop produces and because it is invariant across every start position, trace length and arrival-test variant tested, whereas 5 needs extra gap-memory state.
7) Coverage: fraction of trace samples with any associated AP, times 100, counted over exactly the same 500 samples as the handover count, keeping experiments 4 and 5 consistent.
8) Output formatting follows the existing helper /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result, which renders floats with '%.2f' and ints bare: 91.02, -80.05, 5, 4, 82.00.
9) Nothing in this module needs the Mininet FORWARDING_OVERHEAD constant, Dijkstra tie-breaking, or a compounding-vs-linear overhead choice - those belong to the mininet / p4 / sdn modules and do not enter any of these five values.

result.conventions:
1) OUTPUT FORMATTING (pinned by shipped code): /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py::print_result prints floats as f"{value:.2f}" and everything else bare. So P4_FORWARDING_RATE / P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY / P4_PIPELINE_LATENCY must be floats printing with exactly 2 decimals (922.37, 1.00, 1.50) and P4_TABLE_ENTRIES / P4_MULTICAST_GROUPS must be ints printing bare (16, 5). Returning an int for the accuracy would print '1' and returning floats for the counts would print '16.00'/'5.00'; /workspace/agent_tests/test_mininet_core.py:74-79 shows the house test style is exact string match for ints and abs(float(v) - x) < 0.01 for floats, so type discipline matters.

2) OVERHEAD COMPOSITION - the one contested key, now settled by the repo rather than by taste. The p4 spec defines no P4-specific throughput constant, so P4Switch inherits Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02. All three derivations picked multiplicative but flagged linear (920.00) as a live competitor; that competitor is dead. /workspace/netsim/net.py:245-255 (switch_overhead_factor) already exists and documents 'applied multiplicatively so that N switches yield 0.98 ** N'; /workspace/netsim/node.py names throughput_factor 'Multiplicative'; containernet.yaml defines compute_throughput as 'link_bw * product of all VNF throughput_factors'; utils.compute_path_loss_rate composes per-link factors multiplicatively; and the existing test asserts iperf == 1000 * 0.98 ** 5 with MININET_IPERF_5SW ~= 903.92. I therefore raise P4_FORWARDING_RATE to high confidence at 922.37 and recommend the implementation literally reuse Mininet.iperf / switch_overhead_factor on the P4 topology rather than re-deriving the factor (I ran exactly that: 922.3681599999999).

3) HOP COUNTING: 'through 4 P4 switches' = 4 switch traversals, not 3 inter-switch links and not 5 including host attachments. Verified on the real graph: path('h1','h4') = ['h1','s1','s2','s3','s4','h4'], path_switches = [s1,s2,s3,s4]. Bottleneck bw = min(link_bw) = 1000 is applied before overhead. Hosts contribute no overhead.

4) TOPOLOGY EXACTNESS AND THE hosts-per-switch CHOICE: P4Topology has no default for num_hosts_per_switch, so I take 1, following the documented LinearTopo convention (topo.py: 'k switches, each carrying n hosts', n=1; mininet.yaml: 'k switches, each with one host'). That yields exactly 4 switches + 4 hosts = 8 nodes and 7 links. With 2 hosts/switch it would be 12 nodes / 11 links and P4_TABLE_ENTRIES would double to 32. This is the only place the topology choice leaks into a value.

5) TABLE-POPULATION POLICY: canonical P4 destination forwarding - one ipv4_lpm entry per destination host on EVERY switch, including the locally attached one (4 x 4 = 16). Crucially, the SDN-style 'install rules along each src-dst path' reading is rejected here because that experiment already exists as a separate module (sdn_controller.yaml Experiment 1: ProactiveController.install_all_rules on Tree(depth=2,fanout=3)); duplicating it in the P4 module would be a misreading of 'populating a 4-switch topology with forwarding rules'.

6) PIPELINE LATENCY SCOPE: charged per match-action table only (0.5 us x 3 = 1.5 us), for a single switch. Parser and deparser are free because the spec defines no latency for them, and the experiment is scoped to 'a switch with 3 tables', not to the 4-switch chain.

7) MULTICAST PORT LISTS: the only key where the derivations actually disagreed (5 vs 6). Both are free choices; I took the 2-of-3 majority 3+2 = 5 on the grounds that differently-sized groups are what makes a 'total across 2 groups' measurement meaningful. Together with P4_TABLE_ENTRIES these are the two keys I would write as bounded/API-derived assertions rather than literals.

8) NOT LOAD-BEARING HERE: Dijkstra tie-breaking in netsim/graph.py (the 4-switch chain has a unique shortest path), WiFi handover semantics, and Jain's-index arithmetic all belong to sibling modules. Real-hardware fidelity is also deliberately overridden: a real bmv2 software target sustains only ~100-300 Mbps, but the spec's only rate lever is the inherited 2%/hop constant, so 922.37 is correct for this simulator.

Decisive finding: the "files to create" (netsim/node.py, /workspace/netsim/link.py, /workspace/netsim/topo.py, /workspace/netsim/net.py, /workspace/netsim/experiments/mininet_exp.py) ALREADY EXIST in the round-0 workspace and are complete. `bash /workspace/run.sh` prints exactly: MININET_LINEAR10_NODES: 20 / MININET_TREE_HOSTS: 9 / MININET_IPERF_5SW: 903.92 / MININET_PINGALL_LOSS: 0.00 / MININET_AVG_RTT: 14.67 — identical to the consensus of all three derivations. That makes most "conventions" questions empirical rather than interpretive, and I re-derived every number by hand with exact Fraction arithmetic rather than trusting the code.

Conventions fixed, and why:

1. PER-SWITCH OVERHEAD IS MULTIPLICATIVE (0.98**N), not linear (1 - 0.02*N). This was flagged by all three derivations as the single contested key, each choosing multiplicative at only medium confidence. I resolve it to HIGH on three independent grounds: (a) /workspace/netsim/net.py already ships `switch_overhead_factor()` whose docstring states "Each switch hop costs Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD (2%), applied multiplicatively so that N switches yield 0.98 ** N", and `Switch.throughput_factor` in /workspace/netsim/node.py returns `1.0 - FORWARDING_OVERHEAD` as a per-hop *factor* (a factor composes by multiplication, not subtraction); (b) /workspace/requirements/containernet.yaml line 28 writes the identical per-element modelling problem explicitly as a product — "compute_throughput(): link_bw * product of all VNF throughput_factors" — with line 25 defining `throughput_factor = 1.0 - overhead_pct/100`, structurally the same as Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD; (c) the pre-existing /workspace/netsim/utils.py `compute_path_loss_rate()` composes per-link survival probabilities as a product, establishing multiplicative per-hop composition as the library's house style. Linear would print 900.00; that reading is not supported by any artifact in the repo.

2. OVERHEAD IS CHARGED PER SWITCH TRAVERSED, NOT PER LINK. The h1->h5 path in LinearTopo(k=5) is h1-s1-s2-s3-s4-s5-h5: 6 links but 5 switches. The key name (IPERF_5SW) and the experiment gloss "through 5 switches" pin the exponent at 5, not 6 (885.84) and not 4 (922.37). Confirmed empirically: `path_switches()` returns [s1,s2,s3,s4,s5].

3. IPERF HOST PAIR = FIRST AND LAST HOST (h1, h5). Worth flagging as a live trap: `Mininet.iperf(hosts=None)` in net.py falls through to `client, server = hosts[0], hosts[1]` — i.e. h1-h2, only 2 switches, which would print 960.40. mininet_exp.py correctly passes `[net.hosts[0], net.hosts[-1]]` explicitly. The 5-switch reading is what "through 5 switches" requires.

4. "TOTAL NODES" = HOSTS + SWITCHES, EXCLUDING THE CONTROLLER. `build()` does add c0 (`len(net.controllers) == 1`, verified), but the spec's own parenthetical says "(hosts + switches)" and `Mininet.total_nodes()` is implemented as `len(self.hosts) + len(self.switches)` with the docstring "controllers are not data-plane nodes". containernet.yaml line 35 independently pins the same definition ("total_nodes(): hosts + switches count"). So 20, not 21.

5. TREE SIZING USES MININET'S addTree RECURSION: a node at depth > 0 is a switch with `fanout` children, at depth 0 it is a host, so hosts = fanout**depth and switches = (fanout**depth - 1)/(fanout - 1). Confirmed against the shipped TreeTopo.addTree: Tree(2,3) -> 9 hosts / 4 switches; Tree(2,2) -> 4 hosts / 3 switches with links [(s1,s2),(s1,s3),(s2,h1),(s2,h2),(s3,h3),(s3,h4)].

6. LINK PARAMETERS APPLY TO EVERY LINK, INCLUDING HOST-ACCESS LINKS. This is the second-largest fork (it moves AVG_RTT from 14.67 to 6.67). mininet_exp.py `_build()` passes bw/delay as `**link_opts` into the Topo constructor, which flows through `lopts` to every `addLink`, so all 7 links of LinearTopo(k=4) carry delay=2.0 — verified: [(h1,s1,2.0),(h2,s2,2.0),(h3,s3,2.0),(h4,s4,2.0),(s1,s2,2.0),(s2,s3,2.0),(s3,s4,2.0)]. The spec's "with 2ms link delay" carves out no exception for access links.

7. PING LOSS IS REACHABILITY/CONFIGURED-LOSS BASED, NOT STOCHASTIC. The spec says "Compute loss% via shortest-path reachability"; net.py `ping()` adds 1.0 for an unreachable pair and otherwise `path_loss(path)`. pingall_tree_2_2 sets link_loss: 0.0 explicitly and the tree is connected, so both terms are zero and the result is exactly 0.0 under every pair-counting variant. I did NOT model the first-packet ARP/controller-miss drop that derivation 2 raised as an 8.33 alternative — nothing in the spec or code simulates reactive learning.

8. DIJKSTRA TIE-BREAKING IS A NON-ISSUE FOR ALL FIVE VALUES. `WeightedGraph.shortest_path` minimises HOP COUNT (`nd = d + 1`), ignoring delay and bandwidth; but LinearTopo and TreeTopo are both trees, so every host pair has exactly one simple path and heap pop order cannot change any result. This would only matter in a topology with equal-cost parallel paths (e.g. RingTopo, which ships in topo.py but is unused here).

9. ORDERED VS UNORDERED PAIR AVERAGING DOES NOT MATTER. net.py `ping()` iterates 12 ordered pairs for 4 hosts while `avg_rtt()` iterates 6 unordered pairs; both metrics are symmetric, so 176/12 == 88/6 == 44/3. Verified numerically.

10. FORMATTING FOLLOWS /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py `print_result`: floats via f"{value:.2f}", everything else bare. Node/host counts are Python ints -> "20", "9"; the three measurements are floats -> "903.92", "0.00", "14.67". This resolves the one genuine disagreement among the derivations: derivation 2 gave PINGALL_LOSS as "0.0", but `ping()` returns `100.0 * lost / packets`, a float, so the printed string is "0.00". A test parsing with float() is insensitive to this.

11. NO FREE DESIGN CHOICE affects this module — every value is pinned by the spec text plus the MININET_EXPERIMENTS parameters in configs.py, modulo forks (1) and (6), both of which the shipped code and cross-layer specs resolve consistently. Note configs.py's "linear10" carries link_bw/link_delay that are irrelevant to a node count, and "iperf_linear5" carries link_delay=1.0 that is irrelevant to a bandwidth — these are decoys, not inputs.

Topology: 4 hosts, 4 switches, 7 links — verified all at delay 2.0: (h1,s1),(h2,s2),(h3,s3),(h4,s4),(s1,s2),(s2,s3),(s3,s4). Tree => unique shortest path h_i -> s_i -> ... -> s_j -> h_j with 2 + |i-j| links. Spec defines avg_rtt as "2 * sum of link delays" per pair, so RTT(i,j) = 2 * 2.0 * (2 + |i-j|) = 4*(2 + |i-j|) ms. Six unordered pairs: h1h2 = 12, h1h3 = 16, h1h4 = 20, h2h3 = 12, h2h4 = 16, h3h4 = 12. Sum = 88.0 ms; average = 88/6 = 44/3 = 14.666666... -> "{:.2f}" -> 14.67.
values.alternatives: 6.67 if only the 3 switch-to-switch links carried the 2 ms delay and host-access links were delay-free (4*10/6) — the one substantive fork here, since some LinearTopo implementations shape only the backbone; excluded because mininet_exp._build() passes delay through lopts to every addLink (verified: all 7 links at 2.0) and the spec's "with 2ms link delay" carves out no exception. 7.33 if the round-trip factor 2 were dropped (44/6) — excluded by the explicit "2 * sum of link delays". 29.33 if TCLink's delay were charged on both interfaces of each link (2*88/6), a real netem nuance the spec formula excludes. 20.00 if only the diameter pair h1-h4 were measured instead of averaging. 3.67 if the 1.0 ms configs rows were used instead of linear4_rtt's 2.0. Ordered-pair averaging via all_pairs_shortest_paths gives 176/12 = the identical 14.666..., so pair-counting is not a fork. Precision variants: 14.6667, 14.666666666666666, 15.

values.formula: Topology = TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=3) (confirmed by SDN_EXPERIMENTS["proactive_tree"]={depth:2,fanout:3} in netsim/targets/configs.py and by netsim/topo.py TreeTopo: hosts=f**d=3**2=9, switches=(f**d-1)/(f-1)=(9-1)/2=4, links=12, total nodes=13). Switch names s1 (root), s2/s3/s4 (leaves); hosts h1-h3 on s2, h4-h6 on s3, h7-h9 on s4. ProactiveController.install_all_rules iterates every ORDERED src-dst host pair (9*8 = 72 pairs, matching the existing helper WeightedGraph.all_pairs_shortest_paths which enumerates ordered pairs), and install_path_rules installs exactly one rule per SWITCH on the path (spec: 'Install rules on each switch along path'; hosts have no FlowTable). Path shapes: same-leaf pairs h_i-sX-h_j = 1 switch, there are 3 leaves * (3*2) = 18 such ordered pairs -> 18*1 = 18 rules. Cross-leaf pairs h_i-sX-s1-sY-h_j = 3 switches, 72-18 = 54 ordered pairs -> 54*3 = 162 rules. Total = 18 + 162 = 180. Cross-check per switch: s1 = 54, s2 = s3 = s4 = 42 each (6 intra + 18 outbound + 18 inbound); 54 + 3*42 = 180. FlowTable capacity 4096 >> 54 so no install is rejected. Printed as int -> '180'.
values.alternatives: 90 - if install_all_rules iterates UNORDERED pairs (36) and installs only the forward direction. 360 - unordered pairs but installing both a forward and a reverse rule on each switch (2 per switch per pair). 36 - if match_fields is destination-only AND FlowTable.install replaces/dedupes an identical match (real OpenFlow semantics): each of the 4 switches then holds exactly 9 distinct dst_ip rules = 4*9 = 36. The spec literally says install only rejects 'if at capacity', so no dedup -> 180. 168 - if same-leaf pairs were (wrongly) given 3-switch paths. Free choice noted: nothing in the yaml fixes which src-dst set is used, but 'For every src-dst pair' over all 9 hosts with generate_ip() IPs is the canonical reading.

values.formula: total_install_time() = total_rules_installed() * rule_install_time_ms = 180 * 0.1 ms = 18.0 ms exactly (Python: 180*0.1 == 18.0, no float drift). rule_install_time_ms = 0.1 is fixed by the spec ('Simulated time per rule installation (0.1ms)') and echoed by SDN_EXPERIMENTS["proactive_tree"]["rule_install_time_ms"]=0.1. netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result formats floats with %.2f -> '18.00'.
values.alternatives: 9.00 - if Experiment 1 used unordered pairs (90 rules * 0.1). 3.60 - if rules were deduped to 36 dst-only entries. 0.02 / 0.018 - if the value were reported in seconds instead of ms (spec says ms, so no). 7.20 - if time were charged per PATH (72 paths * 0.1) rather than per rule; the spec says 'time per rule installation', so per-rule. 18.0 vs 18.00 is only a formatting difference; the repo's print_result gives 18.00.

values.formula: The yaml does not name a topology for Exp 3, but netsim/targets/configs.py (being written right now by the sibling mininet agent) has SDN_EXPERIMENTS["link_failure"] = {num_switches: 4, num_hosts_per_switch: 1, failed_link: ('s1','s2')}, and netsim/topo.py adds RingTopo whose docstring says 'A ring gives every switch pair a redundant path, which makes it the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments'. So: RingTopo(k=4, n=1) -> switches s1-s2-s3-s4-s1, hosts h_i on s_i (4 hosts, 12 ordered pairs). Baseline proactive install = 28 rules (8 adjacent-pair paths * 2 switches = 16, plus 4 opposite-pair paths * 3 switches = 12). Then handle_link_failure('s1','s2') removes that edge and, per the spec, 'recompute[s] affected paths' = exactly those stored paths that traversed the s1-s2 edge. With Dijkstra via the existing WeightedGraph.shortest_path (heapq keyed on (dist, node), so ties break to the lexicographically smaller switch name), all four opposite-host paths route over s1-s2, giving 6 affected ordered pairs: (h1,h2) 2->4 switches, (h2,h1) 2->4, (h1,h3) 3->3, (h3,h1) 3->3, (h2,h4) 3->3, (h4,h2) 3->3. Rules reinstalled = 4+4+3+3+3+3 = 20.
values.alternatives: 32 - if handle_link_failure recomputes ALL host pairs instead of only affected ones (post-failure total ring cost: 28 baseline + 4). 17 - pure BFS/insertion-order tie-break (no name ordering): then h4->h2 baselines via s3 and only 5 pairs are affected (4+4+3+3+3). 8 - tie-break that sends every opposite pair the long way round s4 (only h1<->h2 affected, 2 pairs * 4 switches). 6 - if the metric counts recomputed PATHS rather than rules. 16 - if it counts the invalidated rules removed rather than the ones reinstalled. 28 - if 'affected' is defined as any path merely containing endpoint s1 or s2 (10 pairs). If instead Exp 3 reuses the Tree(2,3) of Exp 1 (a tree has no redundancy): 0 under the literal 'reinstall affected paths' reading (nothing is reroutable, true for any failed link), 72 for a full recompute after failing any core s1-sX link, 140 for a full recompute after failing a host link, 108 for the count of invalidated rules. Free choices: which link fails and whether recovery is affected-only or global; I take the config's ('s1','s2') on the ring with affected-only recompute.

values.formula: Spec: 'reactive controller processing 1000 packets with 0.05ms per packet-in' (SDN_EXPERIMENTS["reactive_throughput"] = {num_packets: 1000, packet_in_time_ms: 0.05}). Total simulated controller time = 1000 * 0.05 ms = 50 ms = 0.05 s. Throughput = packet_in_count / elapsed_seconds = 1000 / 0.05 = 20000.0 packet-in events per second. Equivalently 1 / (0.05e-3 s) = 20000/s, so the value is independent of how many packet-ins occur as long as time is accumulated per packet-in. Float -> print_result '%.2f' -> '20000.00'.
values.alternatives: 1440.00 - if the reactive controller only raises a packet-in on a table miss (72 distinct flows in Tree(2,3)) yet the denominator is still the full 1000*0.05 ms = 50 ms wall time (72/0.05). 20.00 - if the rate were reported per millisecond rather than per second. 20000000.00 - if reported per second but with the 0.05 read as microseconds. Note the numeric coincidence that 1000 packets * 0.05 ms = 0.05 s, so 1000/0.05 = 20000 under both the 'divide by seconds' and the naive 'divide by 0.05' readings, which makes 20000 very robust.

values.formula: The yaml fixes nothing here, but SDN_EXPERIMENTS["rule_timeouts"] in netsim/targets/configs.py gives {num_rules: 20, idle_timeout: 10.0, hard_timeout: 0.0, current_time: 15.0, idle_last_matched: 0.0, active_last_matched: 12.0, capacity: 4096}. Two named last-matched values over 20 rules = an even 10/10 split. Idle half: current_time - last_matched = 15.0 - 0.0 = 15.0 >= idle_timeout 10.0 -> expired. Active half: 15.0 - 12.0 = 3.0 < 10.0 -> kept. hard_timeout = 0.0 means permanent, so it never fires. FlowTable.evict_expired(15.0, last_matched_times) removes 20/2 = 10 rules. Printed as int -> '10'. The >= vs > boundary is irrelevant here (15 vs 10, and 3 vs 10).
values.alternatives: 20 - if every one of the 20 rules is given last_matched = 0.0 (no active cohort). 0 - if the eviction experiment reuses the proactive rules from Exp 1: install_path_rules has no timeout parameter, so those rules default to idle_timeout=0/hard_timeout=0 = permanent and nothing can ever be evicted (a strictly literal reading of the spec, and the reason the eviction experiment must build its own rules). 5 - the other common canonical scenario, 10 rules with half carrying a finite idle_timeout. 50 - same half-and-half pattern over 100 rules. 180 - if all Exp 1 rules were installed with an idle_timeout and the clock advanced past it. This value is the least spec-determined of the five; 10 is chosen because it follows directly from the num_rules=20 / idle+active split already committed to configs.py.

result.conventions: Sources and conventions chosen, in order of authority: (1) requirements/sdn_controller.yaml, applied verbatim; (2) requirements/mininet.yaml, which pins TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=3) to 9 hosts (its own MININET_TREE_HOSTS experiment) and therefore 4 switches, 12 links, 13 nodes; (3) the existing helpers netsim/graph.py (WeightedGraph.shortest_path = unit-weight Dijkstra with heapq keyed on (dist, node); all_pairs_shortest_paths enumerates ORDERED pairs) and netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result (ints bare, floats '%.2f'). IMPORTANT CROSS-LAYER FINDING: a sibling agent is concurrently writing netsim/node.py, link.py, topo.py, net.py and has already appended an uncommitted SDN_EXPERIMENTS block to netsim/targets/configs.py. That block is the only thing that pins Experiments 3 and 5, which the yaml leaves entirely open: link_failure = {num_switches: 4, num_hosts_per_switch: 1, failed_link: ('s1','s2')} together with the new RingTopo ('a ring gives every switch pair a redundant path, which makes it the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments'), and rule_timeouts = {num_rules: 20, idle_timeout: 10.0, current_time: 15.0, idle_last_matched: 0.0, active_last_matched: 12.0}. If that file is reverted, Exp 3 and Exp 5 lose their anchors and the alternatives listed for them become live. Specific conventions picked: (a) ORDERED src-dst host pairs, not unordered, for proactive install (72 pairs on the tree, 12 on the ring) — follows 'for every src-dst pair' plus the ordered-pair precedent in all_pairs_shortest_paths; (b) one rule per SWITCH on the path, hosts excluded, and no dedup/replace of identical matches since install only rejects 'if at capacity'; (c) install time is strictly linear, rules * 0.1 ms — the spec gives a flat per-rule cost with no batching, pipelining or per-path component, so no compounding analogue applies here (unlike the mininet layer's per-hop 0.98^N switch overhead); (d) Dijkstra ties broken by lexicographically smaller node name, which is what heapq's (dist, node) tuple ordering yields in the supplied graph.py — this matters only for Exp 3, where it decides whether the four opposite-host ring paths cross s1-s2 (they do: 6 affected pairs, 20 rules) versus a BFS insertion-order tie-break (5 affected pairs, 17 rules); (e) 'rules reinstalled' means rules installed while recomputing only the paths that traversed the failed link, per the literal wording of handle_link_failure ('Remove link, recompute affected paths'), not a global recompute (which would give 32) and not the count of invalidated rules (16); (f) throughput = packet-in events divided by accumulated simulated controller time in seconds, which is invariant to whether all 1000 packets or only the table misses raise packet-ins.

values.formula: Mininet TreeTopo(depth=2, fanout=3) recursion (addTree: switch at depth>0, host at depth 0) gives switches = (f^d - 1)/(f - 1) = (3^2-1)/(3-1) = 4  [s1 root; s2,s3,s4 edge] and hosts = f^d = 3^2 = 9  [h1-h3 on s2, h4-h6 on s3, h7-h9 on s4]; 12 links, 13 nodes total. Verified against /workspace/netsim/topo.py TreeTopo. Proactive install = one flow rule per switch on the path, for every ordered (src_ip, dst_ip) host pair (netsim/graph.py all_pairs_shortest_paths enumerates ordered pairs). Ordered pairs = 9*8 = 72. Intra-edge-switch pairs = 3 groups * (3*2) = 18, path h_i - s_x - h_j -> 1 switch. Inter-group pairs = 72 - 18 = 54, path h_i - s_x - s1 - s_y - h_j -> 3 switches. Total = 18*1 + 54*3 = 18 + 162 = 180. Per-switch check (computed): s1=54, s2=s3=s4=42 -> 54 + 3*42 = 180, all far below FlowTable capacity=4096 so no install is rejected. Printed as int -> "180".
values.alternatives: 90 if install_all_rules iterates UNORDERED pairs (C(9,2)=36 pairs: 9 intra *1 + 27 inter *3 = 90) - i.e. one bidirectional flow per pair. 36 if rules are keyed on dst_ip only (classic destination-based L3 forwarding: each of the 4 switches ends up with exactly 9 dst rules -> 4*9=36), because per-switch duplicates collapse. 360 if install_path_rules installs a forward AND a reverse rule per ordered pair into an append-only table (double counting). 45 if only ingress+egress switch rules were installed for unordered pairs, 72 if only one rule per ordered pair (ingress switch only).

values.formula: total_install_time() = total_rules_installed() * rule_install_time_ms = 180 * 0.1 ms = 18.0 ms. Float arithmetic checked: 180*0.1 == 18.0 exactly and sum(0.1 for _ in range(180)) == 18.0, so no drift. netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result formats floats with %.2f -> "18.00". Convention: cost is linear in rule count, one controller installing rules serially, no separate charge for Dijkstra/path computation and no batching/parallel install.
values.alternatives: 9.00 ms under the unordered-pair convention (90 rules * 0.1). 3.60 ms under dst_ip-only rule keying (36 rules * 0.1). 7.20 ms if the cost were charged per (pair, path) flow-mod message rather than per switch rule (72 pairs * 0.1). 36.00 ms if a barrier/confirm round doubled the per-rule cost. If a per-path computation cost were added (e.g. 0.1 ms per pair) it would be 18.0 + 7.2 = 25.20 ms. Printed as "18" only if the implementation emits an int; the .2f float form is what netsim's print_result produces.

values.formula: FREE DESIGN CHOICE (spec only says "a link failure event"). Canonical choice: a topology with a redundant path, i.e. RingTopo(k=4, n=1) - 4 switches s1..s4 in a ring, one host each (h1..h4), 8 links - which /workspace/netsim/topo.py itself documents as "the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments". Proactive install first: ordered pairs = 4*3 = 12, switch counts per path 2/3/2/2/2/3 per direction -> 28 rules pre-failure (verified). Then handle_link_failure('s1','s2') (the first inter-switch link): with netsim/graph.py Dijkstra (heapq on (dist, name), strict `<` on relaxation, so equal-cost ties resolve toward the lexicographically smaller node popped first) the pre-failure paths crossing s1-s2 are exactly 6 ordered pairs: (h1,h2),(h2,h1) [2 switches each], (h1,h3),(h3,h1) [3 each, routed s1-s2-s3], (h2,h4),(h4,h2) [3 each, routed s2-s1-s4]. After removing s1-s2 the ring becomes the line s2-s3-s4-s1 and the recomputed paths are: h1->h2 = s1,s4,s3,s2 (4), h2->h1 = 4, h1->h3 = s1,s4,s3 (3), h3->h1 = 3, h2->h4 = s2,s3,s4 (3), h4->h2 = 3. Rules reinstalled = 4+4+3+3+3+3 = 20 (computed, not estimated). Printed as int -> "20".
values.alternatives: 0 if the experiment stays on Tree(2,3) (the spec's exp-1 topology): a tree has zero redundancy, so failing any link (s1-s2, or even a host link h1-s2) partitions the graph, every affected flow becomes unreachable and compute_path returns an empty path -> 0 rules reinstalled (36 ordered pairs affected, 108 previously-installed rules invalidated). 108 if the metric is read as "rules invalidated/removed by the failure" on the tree; 16 for the same reading on the ring. 72 if handle_link_failure does a global re-convergence on Tree(2,3) (clear tables, reinstall every still-connected pair: 6+6+6 intra + 54 inter = 72) - a very common lazy implementation of "recompute affected paths". 32 for a global re-convergence on the ring after the failure. 14 or 8 for the ring if a different link fails (s2-s3 or s4-s1 -> 14, s3-s4 -> 8; the asymmetry is purely Dijkstra tie-breaking toward s1/s2, so the choice of failed link is load-bearing). 10 if ring recovery is counted over unordered pairs (4+3+3). 6 if only the two rerouted endpoints/ingress switches are counted rather than all switches on the new paths.

values.formula: Spec fixes both numbers: 1000 packet-in events, 0.05 ms of controller work per packet-in. Simulated elapsed time = 1000 * 0.05 ms = 50 ms = 0.050 s. Throughput = events / elapsed = 1000 / 0.050 = 20000 packet-ins per simulated second. Equivalently 1 / 0.05e-3 s = 20000/s - independent of the 1000 count, since the cost is purely per-event (a Ryu/ONOS-style single-threaded reactive controller at 50 us per packet-in, which is realistic order-of-magnitude). print_result on the float -> "20000.00".
values.alternatives: 20000 (same number, printed as an int if the experiment casts to int). 20.00 if the unit is taken as events per millisecond instead of per second. 6666.67 if the reactive controller is also charged 0.1 ms per installed rule on top of the 0.05 ms packet-in handling for a 1-rule path (1/(0.05+0.1)ms) - and lower still for multi-switch paths, e.g. a 3-switch path costing 0.05+3*0.1 = 0.35 ms gives 2857.14/s. If only table-miss packets counted as packet-ins (a reactive controller installs a rule on the first packet of a flow and the rest are data-plane hits), the count in the numerator drops to the number of distinct flows while elapsed time shrinks proportionally, so the per-second figure stays 20000; only a mixed model (misses charged 0.05 ms, hits charged 0) would change it.

values.formula: FREE DESIGN CHOICE - the spec gives no parameters at all for this experiment (no rule count, no timeout values, no clock advance), and netsim/targets/configs.py has no SDN_EXPERIMENTS block to pin them. Simplest canonical scenario, and the one that actually exercises FlowRule.is_expired / FlowTable.evict_expired selectively: one FlowTable, 10 rules installed, half of them with a finite idle_timeout (e.g. idle_timeout=5 s, installed at t=0 and never re-matched) and half permanent (idle_timeout=0 = never expires, per the spec); advance the simulated clock past the timeout (e.g. current_time=10 s) and call evict_expired -> 10/2 = 5 rules evicted, 5 remain. Printed as int -> "5". This mirrors OpenFlow semantics: idle_timeout=0/hard_timeout=0 rules are permanent and must survive the sweep.
values.alternatives: 10 if all 10 installed rules carry the timeout and all are idle past it (the most degenerate demo), or if the batch is 20 rules with half timing out. 50 if the batch is 100 rules with half expiring (also 100 if all 100 expire). 2 or 3 for a tiny hand-written demo (e.g. 4-6 rules, half expired). 180 if the experiment instead re-uses the exp-1 Tree(2,3) proactive table and gives every rule an idle_timeout - but note install_path_rules has no timeout parameter, so controller-installed rules default to idle_timeout=0/hard_timeout=0 (permanent) and that variant would print 0 unless the experiment builds the rules by hand. A hard_timeout-only convention (evict by install age rather than idle age) yields the same counts for the same split; a convention where an already-evicted rule with both timeouts set is double-counted would inflate the number.

result.conventions:
Topology exactness: I used real Mininet TreeTopo recursion semantics (switch while depth>0, hosts only at depth 0), giving switches=(f^d-1)/(f-1)=4 and hosts=f^d=9 for depth=2/fanout=3 (13 nodes, 12 links) - confirmed both against the mininet.yaml sibling spec (MININET_TREE_HOSTS=9) and against the TreeTopo already present in /workspace/netsim/topo.py (a concurrently-written sibling file).

Pair enumeration: ordered (src,dst) pairs, not unordered. Justification: netsim/graph.py's existing all_pairs_shortest_paths iterates src != dst in both directions, and OpenFlow flow entries are inherently unidirectional (a real controller installs a rule per direction). This doubles exp-1/exp-2 relative to the unordered reading.

Rule granularity: one FlowRule per switch per (src_ip, dst_ip) microflow, matching the install_path_rules(path, src_ip, dst_ip, priority) signature - i.e. exact-match microflow rules like a Ryu simple_switch reactive app, not aggregated destination-based rules. The dst-only aggregation convention would collapse exp 1 from 180 to 36. Rules are installed only on nodes that have a FlowTable (switches); hosts on the path get none. All per-switch counts (max 54) sit below the 4096 capacity, so no install rejection reduces the total.

Cost model: linear, not compounding - total install time = rules * 0.1 ms with a single serial controller, no path-computation charge, no barrier round-trips; controller throughput = events / (events * per-event cost), which makes the per-second figure independent of the 1000-packet count. (A compounding or per-flow-mod-message model is what would change exp 2; see alternatives.)

Dijkstra tie-breaking: netsim/graph.py pushes (dist, node) onto a heapq and only relaxes on strict improvement, so equal-cost ties are won by the lexicographically smaller node name popped first. This is immaterial for Tree(2,3) (paths are unique) but is decisive for the ring in exp 3: the two 2-hop host pairs both route across s1-s2, which is why failing s1-s2 affects 6 ordered pairs (20 rules) while failing s3-s4 affects only 2 (8 rules).

Failure-recovery topology (the one real judgement call): the spec pins Tree(2,3) only for exp 1, and a tree has no redundancy - any link failure partitions it, so an affected-flows-only recovery on the tree necessarily prints 0, and a Mininet/Ryu veteran would not call that a recovery measurement. I therefore assume the canonical minimal redundant topology, a 4-switch ring with one host per switch, and count rules installed for the flows whose path actually used the failed link (real controller behavior: recompute only affected flows). The workspace's own topo.py independently documents RingTopo as the natural link-failure-recovery topology, which is the strongest available signal. The competing conventions (tree + affected-only = 0, tree + global reconvergence = 72, ring + global reconvergence = 32, counting invalidated instead of reinstalled rules = 108) are enumerated in the alternatives.

Output formatting: netsim/experiments/__init__.py print_result renders floats with %.2f and ints bare, so exp 1/3/5 print as bare integers and exp 2 prints "18.00"; exp 4 prints "20000.00" as a float (or "20000" if the implementation casts to int).

values.formula: Config CONTAINERNET_EXPERIMENTS['sfc_chain']: num_vnfs=3, link_bw=1000, vnf_overhead_pct=5.0. Spec: VNF.throughput_factor = 1.0 - overhead_pct/100 = 1.0 - 5.0/100 = 0.95. ServiceFunctionChain.compute_throughput() = link_bw * product(all VNF throughput_factors). Product accumulated first (factor=1.0; factor *= 0.95 three times) = 0.8573749999999999 in IEEE-754; 1000 * that = 857.3749999999999. Exact decimal/rational value is 1000*(19/20)^3 = 6859/8 = 857.375 Mbps. print_result (/workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py) formats floats as '{:.2f}' -> '857.37'. Verified with python3: product-first gives repr 857.3749999999999 -> '857.37'; accumulate-onto-bw gives exactly 857.375 -> '857.38' (round-half-even). Adjudicated to product-first by direct house-style precedent in the ALREADY-IMPLEMENTED /workspace/netsim/net.py: switch_overhead_factor() accumulates factor from 1.0 then iperf() returns 'bw * self.switch_overhead_factor(path)'; I ran net.iperf() on LinearTopo(5) and it returns 960.3999999999999 (not 960.4), i.e. the reference code in this repo demonstrably produces exactly this float artifact for the identical construction. No Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD (0.02) is applied: the SFC formula names only link_bw and VNF factors.
values.alternatives: 857.38 - identical exact math (857.375), different association: accumulating onto the bandwidth (thr=1000.0; thr*=0.95 x3) hits the exactly-representable 857.375, whose round-half-even 2-dp render is 857.38. This is the only real competitor and a tolerance >= 0.01 accepts both; I pick 857.37 on the strength of net.py's implemented accumulate-factor-then-multiply pattern. 857.375 / 857.3750 - the same number if the implementer bypasses print_result's 2-dp formatting (spec says values are printed, and print_result already ships, so 2 dp is expected). 850.00 - linear/additive overhead 1000*(1-3*0.05); ruled out, spec says per-VNF factor and 'product'. 840.23 / 823.42 - additionally charging Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD for 1 or 2 switch hops (857.375*0.98^k); ruled out, that 2%/hop factor belongs to Mininet.iperf and the SFC formula is self-contained. 1000.00 - no VNF derating at all. 285.79 - dividing by num_vnfs. All rejected.

values.formula: Config: num_vnfs=3, link_delay=0.5 ms, vnf_processing_delay=1.0 ms. Spec pins num_links = len(vnfs) + 1 verbatim, with the parenthetical '(includes client->first and last->server)' = 3 + 1 = 4 links. compute_latency() = num_links * link_delay + sum(VNF processing delays) = 4 * 0.5 + (1.0 + 1.0 + 1.0) = 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 ms. Both 0.5 and 1.0 are binary-exact, so the result is exactly 5.0 with no association ambiguity (verified: repr = 5.0). print_result renders the float as '5.00'. One-way, per the spec's closed-form sum; the RTT doubling in Mininet.avg_rtt (/workspace/netsim/net.py) is a different layer's convention and is not applied here.
values.alternatives: 4.00 - num_links = len(vnfs)-1 = 2 (inter-VNF hops only): 2*0.5+3.0; rejected, spec states len(vnfs)+1 literally. 4.50 - num_links = len(vnfs) = 3: 3*0.5+3.0. 7.00 - round-trip on links only (2*2.0+3.0), mirroring net.py's avg_rtt = 2*sum(delays); 10.00 - full RTT doubling of the whole chain. Both rejected: the spec gives an explicit one-way closed form with no factor of 2, and 'end-to-end latency'. 1505.00 / 5.50 - folding DockerHost STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS or per-switch queueing into latency; unsupported by the formula. 2.00 / 3.00 - dropping the VNF or the link term. 5.0 (unformatted) is the same value if print_result is bypassed.

values.formula: Config CONTAINERNET_EXPERIMENTS['resource_fairness']: num_containers=4, cpu_shares=[1024,512,256,256]. Spec: Containernet.compute_resource_fairness() = Jain's fairness index of CPU share allocations. The repo already ships the exact estimator at /workspace/netsim/utils.py:jains_fairness_index(x) = (sum x)^2 / (n * sum x^2), so the implementation is forced. sum = 2048; sum^2 = 4194304. sum of squares = 1048576+262144+65536+65536 = 1441792; n*sum_sq = 4*1441792 = 5767168. J = 4194304/5767168 = 8/11 = 0.7272727272727273. (1) OUTPUT FORMAT. /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py already ships print_result(name, value): floats render as f"{value:.2f}", ints render bare. Every containernet experiment will go through it, so the printed strings are 857.37 / 5.00 / 0.73 / 7 / 50.00. CONTAINER_HYBRID_NODES must be an int so it prints '7', never '7.00'. (2) THROUGHPUT ASSOCIATION ORDER - the main disagreement, resolved empirically. Exact math is unambiguous (857.375) but it lands exactly on a 2-dp rounding tie, so the printed digit depends on multiply order: product-first gives 857.3749999999999 -> '857.37', accumulate-onto-bandwidth gives exactly 857.375 -> '857.38'. Rather than argue from the spec wording alone, I checked the repo's own implemented instance of the identical construction: net.py's switch_overhead_factor() accumulates 'factor = 1.0; factor *= (1.0 - FORWARDING_OVERHEAD)' and iperf() then returns 'bw * self.switch_overhead_factor(path)'. I ran net.iperf() and it returns 960.3999999999999, not 960.4 - the reference code in this repo demonstrably produces exactly this class of float artifact. Combined with the spec's own phrasing ('link_bw * product of all VNF throughput_factors', where the product is a distinct sub-expression), product-first is the faithful reading: 857.37. Flagged medium, not high, because it is a formatting-tie artifact; any checker tolerance >= 0.01 accepts both spellings and only 850.00 (linear overhead) is a genuinely different answer.

(3) MULTIPLICATIVE, NOT LINEAR, VNF OVERHEAD. The spec pins this twice (per-VNF factor = 1 - pct/100, and 'product of all VNF throughput_factors'), and it is the house style: Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD compounds as 0.98^N in net.py. So 1000*0.95^3 = 857.375, never 1000*(1-3*0.05) = 850. All three derivations agreed; I confirm.

(4) NO CROSS-LAYER DOUBLE-CHARGING. The SFC formulas are closed-form over link_bw, link_delay, num_links and VNF parameters only. The 2%-per-switch penalty lives in Mininet.iperf and the container startup penalty lives in DockerHost; folding either into the SFC numbers would double count. Likewise SFC latency is ONE-WAY (5.00), even though net.py's avg_rtt()/rtt() double the link delays - the spec gives an explicit non-doubled sum, and num_links = len(vnfs)+1 = 4 already covers the client and server tail hops.

(5) NODE ACCOUNTING IS NOW CODE-PINNED, NOT TEXT-PINNED. net.py already implements total_nodes() as len(self.hosts) + len(self.switches) with the docstring 'controllers are not data-plane nodes', and addHost() appends to self.hosts. I verified the inherited behaviour live (LinearTopo(10) -> 20, controller excluded despite buildFromTopo creating c0).
